title: The friend between them
hookLine: spring in the forest, Radha sees Krishna dancing with everyone else, and a friend steps in
carry: god searches for the soul too
tomorrow: jnana: to whom did this thought come?

cards: Someone walks into a party looking for one person, and there they are: laughing, surrounded, completely fine. Nobody did anything wrong, exactly. But leaving suddenly looks easier than staying.
That's where Jayadeva's poem puts Radha. It's spring in the forest by the Yamuna. Bees, blossoms, a warm wind from the south.
Radha's friend leads her to a clearing and points: there's Krishna, dancing and playing with all the other gopis.

teach.b: Radha doesn't make a scene. She withdraws, alone into a thicket of vines, hurt and jealous and full of longing all at once. Then the poem does something interesting.

teach.h: KRISHNA LEAVES THE DANCE TO FIND HER.
teach.b: Krishna, in the middle of the dance, suddenly remembers her. He leaves the others to look for her, can't find her, and now he's the miserable one.

So they're apart, each longing for the other, and neither can simply walk across the forest and fix it. That's when Radha's friend, the sakhi, gets to work. She goes to Krishna and describes Radha's grief.
She goes back to Radha and tells her how Krishna is suffering. Back and forth, carrying the messages, softening the hurt, until the two can meet again. Devotees hear layers in this.
Krishna dancing with everyone is God's love for all souls. Radha's hurt is the soul feeling, for a moment, like one among many. Krishna's search says God is not fine without you after all.
That's a core bhakti teaching: the love runs both ways, and God goes looking for the soul too. And the sakhi?
In some Vaishnava traditions, devotees see her as the model of what a teacher or a community does: the friend who carries messages between the soul and God.

teach.h: GOD IS NOT FINE WITHOUT YOU.
teach.b: Some traditions go further and hope for nothing more than to be that friend, serving the love between Radha and Krishna.

teach.h: GOD SEARCHES FOR THE SOUL TOO.
teach.b: One more thing: the poem opens with a hymn to Vishnu's ten descents into the world, and people still sing it on its own.

how: The Gita Govinda's songs are sung in temples and at home, and its opening hymn to Vishnu's ten avatars is often sung on its own; in Vaishnava traditions devotees honor the sakhis, Radha's friends, as models of selfless devotion.

o: a lover's jealousy that you can't control
a song sung only at the temple gate
action, like a friend's work carrying messages

games.q: the spring forest — tap the pairs.
p: left the dance to find her

s: in the poem, Krishna forgets Radha for good
he leaves the dance to search for her. devotees hear God seeking the soul.
Radha's friend carries messages back and forth
the sakhi softens the hurt until the two can meet again.
the Gita Govinda opens with a hymn to Vishnu's ten avatars
and that hymn is still sung on its own.

games.q: you're Radha's friend. Radha is hiding, hurt; Krishna is searching, miserable. what do you do?
o: carry messages between them until they can meet.
games.why: the sakhi goes back and forth, describing each one's longing to the other. some devotees see her as the model of a true friend on the path.

practice: Think of someone who once carried a message for you: a friend who explained you to someone you'd hurt, a teacher who helped you back to something you'd lost, a grandparent who made peace in the family, and thank them silently.
Then, as devotees on this road do, say one name of God you love, Krishna, Rama, Shiva, or simply God, once and slowly, as if answering someone already looking for you.
If you don't pray, just rest in the thought that you're being looked for.

wordCard.voice: Karma, action, is the word these weeks carry. In the Gita Govinda, the action that heals is the friend's: going back and forth until two can meet.

orig.note: Sanskrit: a woman's close friend or companion; Radha's friends in the Gita Govinda.

carryVoice: Your line: God searches for the soul too. Radha hid, Krishna searched, and a friend went back and forth. That's three hundred eighteen days.

sources.ref: Jayadeva, Gita Govinda, cantos 1–6 (the ten avatars hymn; spring; Radha's withdrawal; Krishna's search; the friend's messages)
